rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient to locate the elution window while retaining early compounds and driving late compounds off the column. The retention and resolution pattern will guide window trimming and subsequent slope and temperature tests.

Only one pair is under-resolved, with ample resolution elsewhere and no time penalty. Raise temperature while holding the gradient fixed to test whether temperature-dependent selectivity separates that pair without pushing the last peak beyond 10 minutes.

The close-pair pattern suggests an elution-order reversal between 40 and 50 C, so a further modest temperature increase may open that separation. Test 55 C to balance this gain against the narrowing gap between the peaks currently at 3.76 and 4.04 minutes.

Injection 3 reached the maximum possible CRF and remains the benchmark. Test a shorter gradient at the same temperature to seek a faster fully resolved method and measure how the two marginal pairs respond to gradient steepness.

Preserve injection 3's successful gradient slope of 0.075 organic fraction per minute while trimming the solvent window to shorten retention. This should largely preserve the critical separations, unlike the steeper gradient in injection 4, while testing whether the early peaks remain adequately retained.

Test the cooler side of the apparent critical-pair order reversal with the shorter gradient. Cooling may restore separation without the longer gradient, although other nearby pairs must be checked; injection 3 remains the maximum-score fallback.

Injection 3 already achieves the maximum CRF, so explore a substantially faster alternative. Higher temperature and a steeper gradient may move the narrowing pair through an elution-order reversal into renewed separation, though other pairs may become compressed.

Test whether further steepening opens the reversed pair seen at 60 C and moves the neighboring close pair through its own crossover. This explores a faster selectivity regime while retaining injection 3 as the proven maximum-CRF method.

Return to the successful 55 C selectivity regime and make injection 5's gradient shallower to improve its sole unresolved pair. The higher starting organic fraction may preserve the other critical pair's modest resolution margin, with the last peak still expected before 10 minutes.

Injection 9 achieves maximum CRF but has little resolution margin. Slightly reduce the gradient slope to improve its limiting pair while checking that the other close pair remains resolved and the last peak stays within 10 minutes.

Trim injection 3's unused high-organic range while preserving its starting composition, temperature, and gradient slope exactly. All peaks should elute before the shortened gradient ends at the outlet, preserving maximum CRF with a shorter programmed gradient.

Test whether a higher starting organic fraction improves the nearly slope-insensitive close pair, while a shallower gradient compensates for the separation loss seen for the other critical pair. This seeks greater resolution margin at maximum CRF, with particular attention to early-peak retention and the 10-minute last-peak limit.

Slightly flatten injection 12's gradient to bring its sole unresolved pair above R = 1.5 while retaining the improved separation of the other critical pair. The last peak is expected to remain below 10 minutes, potentially yielding maximum CRF with more resolution margin.

Maximum CRF is already secured; test the low-temperature boundary for an alternative fully resolved method with a shorter gradient. The additional cooling may separate the clustered peaks seen at 35 C through selectivity changes, while the last peak is expected to remain within 10 minutes.

Test whether shifting the starting solvent strength improves selectivity in the fast 60 C regime, where injection 7 had only two unresolved pairs. This explores a faster alternative while retaining the established maximum-CRF methods as fallbacks.

Test a shallower gradient at 60 C to recover the slope-sensitive separation while increasing the temperature-sensitive pair's resolution margin relative to 55 C. The last peak should remain near, but below, 10 minutes; established maximum-CRF methods remain available if this tradeoff fails.

Explore a higher starting organic fraction at 60 C to shift the slope-sensitive pair onto the reversed-order side of its crossover. The moderate gradient slope may preserve neighboring separations better than the fast gradients tested previously, while keeping retention well below 10 minutes.

Raise the starting organic fraction while preserving injection 17's slope to test whether the reversed critical pair opens sufficiently for a faster maximum-CRF method. Check the first pair carefully, since its separation may now become limiting as early retention decreases.

Return to injection 13's fully resolved selectivity and increase its gradient slope slightly, from 0.045 to 0.046875 per minute. This should shorten the last-peak retention while preserving some of its resolution margin; injection 11 remains the fastest proven maximum-CRF method.

Use a slope midway between the fully resolved injections 9 and 10, with a trimmed endpoint and shorter programmed gradient. Both critical pairs should remain above R = 1.5, and the last peak should elute around 8 minutes before the gradient ends at the outlet.

Test whether a steeper gradient at 40 C opens the sole critical pair from injection 1 while retaining sufficient separation elsewhere. This explores a faster selectivity regime than the proven 55 C methods, which already secure the maximum CRF.

Preserve the proven gradient slope through all nine early peaks, then test a lower-organic hold for the isolated last compound. This may retain maximum CRF with a shorter programmed gradient and lower final organic fraction, provided the last peak still elutes within 10 minutes.

Test a slightly shallower slope than injection 10 to establish how much gradient variation the maximum-CRF separation tolerates. The slope-sensitive pair should improve, while the other critical pair and the last-peak time will determine the usable boundary.

Test a slope of 0.0667 per minute, just steeper than injection 9, to locate the fastest fully resolved boundary at this starting composition. The limiting pair may fall slightly below R = 1.5, but the established maximum-CRF methods remain secured.

Finish with a gradient slope between the fully resolved injections 13 and 19, targeting balanced resolution margins and a last peak below 10 minutes. Maximum CRF is already secured; injection 11 remains the fastest proven fully resolved method.
